title: Pixar Films
text:
For this part, I decided to explore the connection of different ratings for the Pixar films. The dataset comes from the pixarfilms R package by Eric Leung, which compiles information primarily sourced from Wikipedia. The dataset includes details about each film’s title, Rotten Tomatoes score, Metacritic score, Cinema Score, and Critics Choice score.


Show code
library(ggplot2)
library(tidytuesdayR)
tuesdata <- tidytuesdayR::tt_load(2025, week = 10)
public_response <- tuesdata$public_response


head(public_response)


# A tibble: 6 × 5
  film            rotten_tomatoes metacritic cinema_score critics_choice
  <chr>                     <dbl>      <dbl> <chr>                 <dbl>
1 Toy Story                   100         95 A                        NA
2 A Bug's Life                 92         77 A                        NA
3 Toy Story 2                 100         88 A+                      100
4 Monsters, Inc.               96         79 A+                       92
5 Finding Nemo                 99         90 A+                       97
6 The Incredibles              97         90 A+                       88




Show code
# Create a scatterplot comparing Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic scores
public_response |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = rotten_tomatoes, y = metacritic)) +
   # Plot each movie as a point, remove rows with missing values
  geom_point(na.rm = TRUE) +
  # Add a smooth LOESS curve to show the overall trend 
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, color = "black")+
  # Add a title and axis labels
  labs(title= "Rotten Tomatoes vs. Metacritic Scores for Pixar Movies", 
       x = "Rotten Tomatos score", 
       y = "Metacritic Score")+
  theme_classic()





Relationship between Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic scores for Pixar films, with a trend line showing how higher Rotten Tomatoes ratings generally correspond to higher Metacritic scores.




The scatterplot shows a strong positive relationship between Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic scores for Pixar films. As Rotten Tomatoes ratings increase, Metacritic scores tend to rise as well, although the pattern isn’t perfectly linear. Overall the trend suggests that Pixar movies that perform well with one rating system generally perform well with the other too.
Source:
R4DS Online Learning Community. “TidyTuesday.” https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main.
R4DS Online Learning Community. “Pixar Movies Dataset.” https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2025/2025-03-11.
Original data source citation (Pixar)
Leung, Eric. “pixarfilms R Package.” Data sourced primarily from Wikipedia. https://github.com/erictleung/pixarfilms.

title: Gas Prices in the US
text:
For this project, I decided to look at the change of price for Gas (2 types - diesel and Gasoline). The dataset is from U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), who updates price information weekly. The dataset includes information on the date, fuel type, grade, formulation, and price.


Show code
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytuesdayR)
tuesdata <- tidytuesdayR::tt_load(2025, week = 26)

weekly_gas_prices <- tuesdata$weekly_gas_prices
weekly_gas_prices <-weekly_gas_prices |> 
   mutate(year = year(ymd(date)))

head(weekly_gas_prices)


# A tibble: 6 × 6
  date       fuel     grade   formulation  price  year
  <date>     <chr>    <chr>   <chr>        <dbl> <dbl>
1 1990-08-20 gasoline regular all           1.19  1990
2 1990-08-20 gasoline regular conventional  1.19  1990
3 1990-08-27 gasoline regular all           1.25  1990
4 1990-08-27 gasoline regular conventional  1.25  1990
5 1990-09-03 gasoline regular all           1.24  1990
6 1990-09-03 gasoline regular conventional  1.24  1990




Show code
#| fig-cap: The weekly change in Gas price over the years from 1990 to 2025

#| fig-alt: The linegraph shows years (ranging from 1990 to 2025) on the x-axis, and price per gallon USD (ranging from 0 to 4.5) on the Y axis. There are two lines, one for the gas type- diesel, and another one for the gas type - gasoline. The graph shows that the gas price for both types was steady and hovered around 1 USD untill 2000. After 2000, untill 2012, the gas price experiences dramatic increase, reaching around 3.7 USD for diesel. Gasoline follows the price of diesel untill 2016, after which it still increases, but at a lower rate than diesel. Both types get cheaper, and reach the low point around 2017 at 2.5 USD. After 2017 both types go up in price again, and in 2022 avarage price of diesel is higher than 4 USD, and price of gasoline is around 3.7 USD. After 2022, both types experience another slight price decrease. 


weekly_gas_prices |> 
  # X axis is the years, and the Y axis is the price per gallon. Each line represents fuel type.
  ggplot(aes(x= year, y= price, color = fuel)) +
  geom_smooth()+
  # Labels for the axes and the legend
  labs(
    title = "Gas Price Trends Over Time",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Price (USD per gallon)",
    caption = "Source: TidyTuesday (2025) Weekly US Gas Prices", 
    color = "Gas Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









The graph shows how gas prices have shifted over time. Both types stay fairly steady from 2000 to 2010, then jump sharply between 2010 and 2012 and again from 2017 to 2022. Prices dip a bit from 2010 to 2017 and after 2022, although they never return to their original levels. Looking at the two lines separately, gasoline remains the cheaper option, especially during the major spikes in 2022–2023.
Sources:
R4DS Online Learning Community. “TidyTuesday.” https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main.
R4DS Online Learning Community. “Gas Price Dataset.” https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2025/2025-07-01.
Original data source citation (US gas prices)
U.S. Energy Information Administration. “Weekly Retail Gasoline and Diesel Prices.” https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/gasdiesel.

title: Data Ethics
text:
In 2014, Amazon began developing an automated system to assist with resume screening. The goal was to manage large applicant pools more efficiently and create a consistent evaluation process. Engineers trained the model on a decade of historical hiring data, assuming that patterns in past decisions would reveal which skills and experiences Amazon valued. The system was also expected to reduce subjectivity by standardizing how resumes were scored.
By 2018, Amazon discontinued the project. Reporting from Reuters shows that the model learned gender-correlated patterns from the historical data rather than neutral indicators of qualification (Reuters, 2018). Because the majority of past applicants were men, the algorithm interpreted male-associated terms as stronger signals of competence. It penalized resumes containing phrases like “women’s,” downgraded applicants from women’s colleges, and rewarded language more common in male-dominated fields. The model never explicitly used gender as a feature, but its reliance on proxy variables reproduced existing inequities in Amazon’s hiring history.
Anti-discrimination law prohibits employers from making decisions based on gender, even indirectly. Once the bias was detected, discontinuing the model became necessary. However, the broader trend toward automated hiring accelerated regardless. A 2024 Gallup report found that the vast majority of Fortune 500 HR leaders had already integrated some form of AI into their hiring workflows (Gallup, 2024). Concerns about transparency and fairness remain widespread. In 2024, Derek Mobley filed a discrimination lawsuit against Workday, alleging that its algorithmic screening system rejected applicants in ways that disproportionately harmed job seekers based on race, age, and disability (Forbes, 2025).
Amazon continues to incorporate AI-based tools in parts of its hiring pipeline, but the company has provided limited public detail about how these systems operate or how they are evaluated for bias. The situation highlights a clear tension: the data science component is the machine-learning model that identifies patterns in past hiring decisions, while the ethical challenge lies in the model’s tendency to reproduce existing biases and its lack of transparency to those affected by automated decisions.

From Data Values and Principles manifesto
As data teams, we aim to…

Principle 1 — Use data to improve life for our users, customers, organizations, and communities.

Amazon’s statement on their AI use in hiring reads - 
“Over the last several years, we’ve built tools using AI and ML to help job applicants throughout the hiring process—from identifying the right position to apply for, to giving them more flexibility through online assessments that help us engage and evaluate candidates—all while driving equity and fairness in the hiring process and adhering to legal standards.” (Amazon Staff, 2025)
AI systems used in hiring are often promoted as tools that can streamline screening and reduce subjectivity (EEOC, 2023). However, the outcome is drastically different from the anticipated utopia. In Amazon’s case, women were penalized for using terms that linked to their gender, such as attending all-women’s colleges or leading women’s clubs. This outcome was unintended and accidental – the workers creating the model never would have expected that the system they built would discriminate on that basis. But still, the effect is clear – the model created to eliminate human bias only contributed to upholding it. This is damaging to everyone involved – women workers are unfairly rejected, and Amazon misses out on highly qualified candidates. As an organization, Amazon is committed to upholding values of fairness and inclusivity, and models like these contradict those ideals.



Principle 7 — Recognize and mitigate bias in ourselves and in the data we use

The backlash from the initial reporting spread far beyond the tech world, and conversations about AI ethics quickly moved into the mainstream. While Amazon never released full details about its hiring model, reporting from Reuters makes clear that the system exhibited gender-related bias because it learned patterns from historical resume data rather than from explicitly encoded rules (Reuters, 2018). When asked about the tool, an Amazon spokesperson declined to comment on its specific failures and emphasized that the model had never been used to make final hiring decisions.
The underlying issue was not that Amazon intentionally designed a sexist model, but that the system reflected patterns in the company’s own historical hiring practices. Because the model was trained on a decade of resumes submitted to Amazon, it identified male-associated terms as stronger signals of qualification than female-associated ones. This kind of outcome is common when machine-learning systems ingest biased datasets (Bogen & Rieke, 2018). Acknowledging this publicly would have required Amazon to confront long-standing inequities in its own hiring pipeline.
Transparency and accountability are essential for building trust in automated hiring systems, yet Amazon provided limited visibility into how the model operated or why it failed. Although the company ultimately discontinued the system, it has not released meaningful details about what was learned from the incident or how similar risks will be addressed going forward.



Principle 10 — Respect and invite fair criticism while promoting the identification and open discussion of errors, risks, and unintended consequences of our work.

Amazon’s handling of its hiring model reflects a clear breakdown of this principle. After internal teams discovered that the model exhibited gender-related bias, the company provided very little public explanation about what went wrong or how the issue was addressed. The system was never released for independent auditing, and researchers had no opportunity to examine the model’s behavior or identify where the bias originated. Instead of encouraging open discussion, Amazon offered minimal commentary and framed the tool as an experiment that was never fully deployed. This reluctance to engage with external critique prevented meaningful public scrutiny, limited the possibility of fixing underlying problems, and weakened trust in the company’s broader use of AI in hiring.



Principle 6: Be open to changing our methods and conclusions in response to new knowledge.

With experimental and breakthrough work, some complications are inevitable. The same can be said for Amazon’s hiring model. While the system remains private and its training data unavailable to the public, Reuters reported that Amazon’s team had edited the model to reduce gender bias. Still, the underlying issue persists. The logic behind AI decision-making is often opaque, and identifying bias requires extensive testing and transparency. At present, it’s impossible to know what specific factors the model may use to discriminate against candidates. There are countless subtle ways for an AI to reproduce human bias – through zip codes, first and last names, student organizations, or even languages spoken.
Amazon acknowledges this risk, stating:
“As part of this process, we start with user research—diving deep to understand the context for our tools from diverse and representative perspectives and experiences. Prior to launching any new tool, we conduct studies ensuring that the tool is similarly benefiting individuals from diverse identity groups.”
However, despite this apparent commitment to equity, it remains unclear what concrete steps the company has taken to ensure that past mistakes are not repeated.




Summary
Amazon’s hiring model highlights how easily AI systems can inherit and amplify human bias. The company’s lack of transparency and resistance to outside scrutiny reveal how easy it is for bias to remain hidden behind claims of progress. As artificial intelligence becomes a standard part of hiring practices, the consequences of these systems grow even more significant. With recent cases like the lawsuit against Workday’s AI screening system, it becomes clear that these issues are not isolated mistakes but symptoms of a larger problem. Taking them seriously is crucial, as fairness and accountability must remain at the center of technological advancement.


Citations

Main Sources
Dastin, J. (2018, October 11). Insight – Amazon scraps secret AI recruiting tool that showed bias against women. Reuters.
https://www.reuters.com/article/us-amazon-com-jobs-automation-insight-idUSKCN1MK08G/
Amazon Staff. (2025, November 4). How Amazon leverages AI and ML to enhance the hiring experience for candidates. About Amazon.
https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/workplace/how-amazon-leverages-ai-and-ml-to-enhance-the-hiring-experience-for-candidates


Supporting Sources
Gallup (2024, October 7). AI in the workplace: Answering 3 big questions.
https://www.gallup.com/workplace/651203/workplace-answering-big-questions.aspx
Gassam Asare, J. (2025, June 23). What the Workday lawsuit reveals about AI bias—and how to prevent it. Forbes.
https://www.forbes.com/sites/janicegassam/2025/06/23/what-the-workday-lawsuit-reveals-about-ai-bias-and-how-to-prevent-it/
U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. (2023). Assessing algorithmic fairness in employment selection. https://www.eeoc.gov/
Bogen, M., & Rieke, A. (2018). Help Wanted: An Examination of Hiring Algorithms, Equity, and Bias. Upturn. https://www.upturn.org/reports/2018/hiring-algorithms/

title: Data Science final presentation
text:
Helper function

get_movie_info <- function(title, year = NULL) {
  
  #Where I'm getting the information
  base_url <- "http://www.omdbapi.com/"
  
  # Build the query parameters
  #'t' is the movie title, 'apikey' is my personal API key
  params <- list(
    apikey = omdb_api_key,
    t = title )
  
  # If a year is provided, add it to the query
  if(!is.null(year)) {
    params$y = year}
  
  # Send GET request to the API
  res <- GET(url = base_url, query = params)
  
  #Output in case of an HTTP error
  if (http_error(res)) {
    warning(paste("Request failed for:", title))
    return(tibble(
      title = NA_character_,
      author = NA_character_,
      subject = NA_character_,
      category = NA_character_,
      publisher_location = NA_character_,
      publish_date = NA_character_,
      response = "HTTP error"
    ))}
  
  
    # Convert convert from JSON (which OMDB uses) to R list
    # format the date
  txt <- content(res, "text", encoding = "UTF-8")
  data <- fromJSON(txt)
  release_date <- as.Date(data$Released, format = "%d %b %Y")
  date_formatted <- format(release_date, "%b/%d/%Y")  
  
  #If the movie was not found
  if (identical(data$Response, "False")) {
    return(tibble(
      title = NA_character_,
      author = NA_character_,
      subject = NA_character_,
      category = NA_character_,
      publisher_location = NA_character_,
      publish_date = NA_character_,
      response = data$Error
    ))}
  
  
  #If found, return the tibble with the information
  tibble(
    title = data$Title,
    author = data$Director,
    subject = data$Language,
    category = data$Genre,
    publisher_location = data$Country,
    publish_date = date_formatted,
    response = "OK")}

title: Data Science final presentation
The Rise of AI in BBC article titles
text:
Show code
library(RTextTools) 
library(tidyverse)
library(stringr)
library(readr)
library(lubridate)
library(data.table)
articles <- read.csv("bbc_news.csv")


For the purpose of analysis, I compiled a list of AI-related terms to make the search process easier.


Show code
ai_terms <- "(ai|artificial intelligence|machine learning|deep learning|neural network|chatgpt|openai|gpt[- ]?\\d|large language model|llm)"


The titles in the dataset were converted to lowercase, and all AI-related terms from the original list were replaced with the placeholder “ai” to simplify analysis. In this context, “ai” represents any term referring to artificial intelligence (e.g., machine learning, chatgpt, neural networks). Additionally, the publication dates were converted from character strings to date variables for easier grouping.


Show code
# Clean article titles
articles <- articles |> 
  mutate(
    # Ensure titles are character strings
    title = as.character(title),
    # Convert titles to lowercase 
    lower_title = str_to_lower(title),
    # Replace all AI-related terms with the token "ai"
    lower_title = str_replace_all(lower_title, ai_terms, "ai"),
    # Create a variable showing whether "ai" appears or not
    topic_ai = str_detect(lower_title, "\\bai\\b"))

# Convert publication dates 
articles <- articles |> 
  mutate(
    # Parse publication dates into datetime format and extract the year and month
    clean_date = dmy_hms(pubDate),
    year_month = format(clean_date, "%Y-%m"))


Although the dataset predominantly contains articles published between 2022 and 2024, one older article from 2013 appeared during parsing. Since it falls outside the time range of interest, it was removed for consistency. The histogram below shows the distribution of publication dates after filtering, showing the time span covered in the analysis.


Show code
articles |> 
  # Plot a histogram
  ggplot(aes(x = clean_date)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "skyblue",
    color = "white") +
  # Make x-axis range from 2022 to 2024 in order to remove outlier article
  scale_x_datetime(limits = c(as.POSIXct("2022-01-01"), as.POSIXct("2024-12-31"))) +
  # Add title and axis labels
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of BBC Article Publication Dates",
    x = "Publication Date",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_light()





Distribution of BBC article publication dates from 2022 to 2024, showing the number of articles published over time.






Show code
# Create monthly counts of AI-related articles
articles_month <- articles |> 
  # Filter by AI mentions
  filter(topic_ai) |> 
  # Group by month
  group_by(year_month)|> 
  # Count numbers
  summarize(number = n()) |> 
  # Create a clean date variable
  mutate(year_month = as.Date(paste0(year_month, "-01")))
  
# Plot AI mentions over time
articles_month |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year_month, y = number)) +
  # Line showing trend over time
  geom_line(color = "#FFF59D", size = 1.2)+
  # Points colored by magnitude of AI mentions
  geom_point(aes(color = number), size = 2.5)+
  # Color gradient
  scale_color_gradient(low = "#FFF59D", high = "#E53935")+
  # Add title and axis labels
  labs(title = "AI Mentions by Month",
    subtitle = "Tracking the rise of AI-related articles over time",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of AI Articles") +
  # Format x-axis as months
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %Y", date_breaks = "5 months") +
  theme_light()





This plot shows how often BBC articles mentioned AI each month.






Show code
# AI mentions grouped by year and month
year_month <- articles |>
  mutate(yr = year(clean_date), mnth = month(clean_date)) |>
  group_by(yr, mnth) |>
  summarise(ai_mentions = sum(topic_ai))

# Plot heatmap of AI mentions
year_month |> 
  # remove the outlier article
  filter(yr>2021) |> 
  mutate(mnth = factor(mnth, levels = 1:12, labels = month.abb)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = mnth, y = yr, fill = ai_mentions)) +
  # Heatmap tiles
  geom_tile() +
  # Color gradient
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#FFF59D", high = "#E53935") +
  # Add title and axis labels
  labs(title = "Heatmap of AI mentions by year and month", x = "Month", y = "Year", fill = "Count") +
  theme_light()





Heatmap showing the number of AI-related BBC articles across months and years. Darker colors indicate months with higher frequencies of AI mentions.




The line graph and the Heatmap show the number of BBC articles mentioning AI-related terms in their titles from May 2022 to January 2024. The data reveals an initial rise in mentions around April and May 2023, followed by a second peak in November 2023. The first surge corresponds to the public release of GPT-4 and the growing media attention surrounding generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot. The later spike in November aligns with OpenAI’s Dev Day announcements and the coverage of the company’s leadership changes. Overall, 2023 had the highest number of AI-related articles in the dataset, indicating a significant rise of media attention.


Show code
# Extract and count the most common words that appear immediately after "ai"
articles_word <- articles |>
  # Keep only AI-related articles
  filter(topic_ai) |> 
  # Extract the word following "ai"
  mutate(ai_word = str_extract(lower_title, "(?<=ai )\\w+")) |> 
  filter(!is.na(ai_word)) |> 
  # Group by the extracted word
  group_by(ai_word) |> 
  # Count how many times each word appears
  summarize(number_of_mentions = n()) |> 
  select(ai_word, number_of_mentions) |> 
  # Sort by most frequent words and keep top 15
  arrange(desc(number_of_mentions)) |> 
  slice_head(n = 15)

# Extract and count the most common adjectives that follow "ai is"
articles_adj <- articles |>
   # Keep only AI-related articles and extract the word following "ai"
  filter(topic_ai) |> 
  mutate(ai_word = str_extract(lower_title, "(?<=ai is )\\w+")) |> 
  filter(!is.na(ai_word)) |> 
  # Group by the extracted adjective
  group_by(ai_word) |> 
  # Count how many times each word appears
  summarize(number_of_mentions = n()) |> 
  select(ai_word, number_of_mentions) |> 
  # Sort by most frequent words
  arrange(desc(number_of_mentions))




Show code
# Bar plot
articles_word |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = ai_word, y = number_of_mentions)) +
  # Flip coordinates so words appear on the y-axis (more readable)
  geom_col(fill = "forestgreen") +
  coord_flip() +
  # Ensure y-axis uses integer tick marks only
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_width(1))+
  # Add title and axis labels
  labs(
    title = "Most Common Words Following 'AI'",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_light()





Most common words appearing directly after “AI” in BBC article titles, based on the top 15 extracted terms from AI-related headlines.






Show code
# Bar plot
articles_adj |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = ai_word, y = number_of_mentions)) +
  # Flip coordinates so words appear on the y-axis (more readable)
  geom_col(fill = "coral") +
  coord_flip() +
  # Ensure y-axis uses integer tick marks only
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_width(1)) +
  # Add title and axis labels
  labs(
    title = "Most Common Words Following 'AI is'",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_light()





Most common words appearing after the phrase “AI is” in BBC article titles




To explore how AI is used in context, I created two graphs showing the words that most frequently follow the placeholder term “ai”, and the words that follow the phrase “ai is”. I filtered the dataset to include only titles containing AI-related terms and used lookarounds to extract the surrounding words.
The first graph shows that the most common words following ai are “is,” “to,” “could,” and “in.” This pattern makes sense given the normal sentence structures in article titles, where ai often acts as a subject followed by verbs or prepositions.
The second graph focuses on words that appear after “ai is.” The most frequent one is “helping” (appearing twice), followed by single occurrences of words like “terrifying,” “not,” “most,” “matching,” “lying,” “hateful,” and “being.” It’s interesting that most of the adjectives carry a negative tone, reflecting the media narratives around AI, which emphasize fear, uncertainty, or ethical concerns over generative AI
Citation:
BBC News. “BBC News Articles.” Dataset compiled from publicly available BBC News RSS feeds and APIs, covering articles published from March 2022 to July 2024. https://www.bbc.com/news.
Kikadara, Bhavik. BBC News Articles Dataset. Kaggle, 2024. https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/bhavikjikadara/bbc-news-articles.

title: Data Wrangling with SQL
text:
Introduction
In this analysis, I examine traffic stop data from three cities to understand how race and gender shape who gets stopped. All data wrangling is done in SQL, including extracting racial distributions, proportions of stops within each city, and demographic patterns across groups. I also incorporate external population data to compare stop patterns to the cities’ underlying demographic makeup. The final plots and tables highlight clear differences across cities and provide a basis for interpreting how stop patterns vary by group.


Data Wrangling
Establishing the connection:


Show code
con_traffic <- DBI::dbConnect(

  RMariaDB::MariaDB(),

  dbname = "traffic",

  host = Sys.getenv("TRAFFIC_HOST"),

  user = Sys.getenv("TRAFFIC_USER"),

  password = Sys.getenv("TRAFFIC_PWD")

)


Loading libraries:


Show code
library(DBI)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)


Before diving into the SQL analysis, it’s useful to look at the overall size of the dataset across the three cities. The bar chart below shows the total number of traffic stops recorded in Los Angeles, Austin, and Nashville. Seeing the relative scale of each dataset helps provide context for the later comparisons by race and gender, since the number of stops varies considerably from city to city.


Show code

# Total stops in Los Angeles
SELECT 'Los Angeles' AS city, COUNT(*) AS num_stops
FROM ca_los_angeles_2020_04_01

UNION ALL

# Total stops in Austin
SELECT 'Austin' AS city, COUNT(*) AS num_stops
FROM tx_austin_2020_04_01

UNION ALL

# Total stops in Nashville
SELECT 'Nashville' AS city, COUNT(*) AS num_stops
FROM tn_nashville_2020_04_01;




Show code
#| fig-alt: Bar chart showing the total number of traffic stops in three cities: Los Angeles has the highest count, Nashville has the second highest, and Austin has the smallest dataset.

# Create a bar chart showing total stops per city
stops_by_city |>
  ggplot(aes(x = city, y = num_stops, fill = city)) +
  # Titles and axis labels, remove legend
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Number of Traffic Stops by City",
    x = "City",
    y = "Number of Stops"
  ) +
  theme_bw()





A bar chart showing total number of traffic stops recorded in Los Angeles, Austin, and Nashville.




Extracting the proportions of stops in Los Angeles, Austin, and Nashville by race:


Show code

# Compute the number of stops for each race in each city
SELECT
  race_count.subject_race,
  race_count.city,
  race_count.n,
  race_count.n * 1.0 / total.total AS prop
FROM (
  -- Count stops by race in Los Angeles
    SELECT 
        subject_race,
        COUNT(*) AS n,
        'Los Angeles' AS city
    FROM ca_los_angeles_2020_04_01
    GROUP BY subject_race

    UNION ALL

    -- Count stops by race in Austin
    SELECT 
        subject_race,
        COUNT(*) AS n,
        'Austin' AS city
    FROM tx_austin_2020_04_01
    GROUP BY subject_race

    UNION ALL

    -- Count stops by race in Nashville
    SELECT 
        subject_race,
        COUNT(*) AS n,
        'Nashville' AS city
    FROM tn_nashville_2020_04_01
    GROUP BY subject_race

) AS race_count

-- Compute total stops per city (needed to calculate proportions)
JOIN (
    SELECT 'Los Angeles' AS city, COUNT(*) AS total
    FROM ca_los_angeles_2020_04_01

    UNION ALL

    SELECT 'Austin', COUNT(*)
    FROM tx_austin_2020_04_01

    UNION ALL

    SELECT 'Nashville', COUNT(*)
    FROM tn_nashville_2020_04_01
) AS total
ON race_count.city = total.city
-- Sort
ORDER BY race_count.city, race_count.subject_race;


I used the join because the race counts and the total counts require two different levels of aggregation. The race_count subquery groups by race, while the total subquery counts all stops in each city. Joining them lets me compute n / total cleanly. Since MySQL on Posit doesn’t allow window functions in this setup, the join is the simplest valid approach.
Extracting the number of stops in Austin based on gender:


Show code

-- the number of stops in austin based on gender

-- Count stops by race for female subjects
(SELECT 
    subject_race, 
    count(*) as n, 
    "female" as sex
  FROM tx_austin_2020_04_01
  WHERE subject_sex = "female"
  GROUP BY subject_race)
  
  UNION ALL

-- Count stops by race for male subjects
(SELECT 
    subject_race, 
    count(*) as n,
    "male" as sex
  FROM tx_austin_2020_04_01
  WHERE subject_sex = "male"
  GROUP BY subject_race)
  
-- Sort
ORDER BY subject_race, sex


Extracting the average number of people who were stopped in Austin by gender:


Show code

-- number of stops in austin based on gender and age

-- Average age by race for female subjects
(SELECT 
    subject_race, 
    AVG(subject_age) as age, 
    "female" as sex
  FROM tx_austin_2020_04_01
  WHERE subject_sex = "female"
  GROUP BY subject_race)
  
  UNION ALL

-- Average age by race for male subjects
(SELECT 
    subject_race, 
    AVG(subject_age) as age,
    "male" as sex
  FROM tx_austin_2020_04_01
  WHERE subject_sex = "male"
  GROUP BY subject_race)
  -- Sort
ORDER BY subject_race, sex


To compare stop rates with the underlying demographics of each city, I used racial population estimates from the 2020 U.S. Census, accessed through the CensusDots database. The Census provides city-level counts for major racial categories, which I matched to Los Angeles, Austin, and Nashville. These population values reflect the residential makeup of each city in 2020, allowing me to compare the racial distribution of stopped drivers to the racial distribution of the city’s population in the same period.
Dataframe with the population distribution in Los Angeles, Austin, and Nashville:


Show code
population_data <- data.frame(
  city = c(
    "Los Angeles", "Los Angeles", "Los Angeles", "Los Angeles", "Los Angeles",
    "Austin",  "Austin",   "Austin",   "Austin",   "Austin", 
    "Nashville",  "Nashville",  "Nashville",  "Nashville", "Nashville"
  ),
  subject_race = c(
    "asian/pacific islander",
    "black",
    "hispanic",
    "other",
    "white",

    "asian/pacific islander",
    "black",
    "hispanic",
    "other",
    "white",

    "asian/pacific islander",
    "black",
    "hispanic",
    "other",
    "white"
  ),
  n = c(
    14.7, 7.6,  48, 41, 25.6,    #Los Angeles
    8.9, 6.9, 32.5, 4.7, 47.1,    # Austin
    3.9, 24.3, 14, 4.5, 53.3    # Nashville
  )
)




Data Visualisation


Show code
# Plot the proportion of traffic stops by race for each city.
city_race_prop |> 
  filter(!is.na(subject_race), subject_race != "unknown") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = subject_race, y = prop, fill = subject_race)) +
  geom_col() +
  # Using facet_wrap lets us compare racial distributions across cities.
  facet_wrap(~ city) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.title.x = element_blank()
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Paired") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Stopped Individuals by Race",
    y = "Proportion of stops",
    fill = "Race of Subject"
  )





Bar graph of proportion of traffic stops by race across Austin, Los Angeles, and Nashville.




This graph shows the distribution of individuals stopped by the police in 3 cities – Los Angeles, Austin, and Nashville. Looking at the graph, there seems to be significant race differences – for example, in Austin and Los Angeles, it is predominately white and hispanic individuals who are stopped. In Nashville, the largest groups are white and Black individuals. However, we should be careful when it comes to arriving to conclusions from this graph. To understand the full picture, we need to compare these stop patterns to the general racial makeup of each city.


Show code
 # population counts by race for each city
population_data |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = subject_race, y = n, fill = subject_race)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ city) +
  theme_bw() +
  # Remove x-axis labels
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.title.x = element_blank()
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Paired") +
  labs(
    title = "Population Distriburion by Race",
    y = "Percentage",
    fill = "Race of Subject"
  )





Population distribution by race across Austin, Los Angeles, and Nashville.




Once we compare the stop data to the general population, the picture gets clearer. In Austin, the racial breakdown of stopped individuals closely mirrors the city’s demographics. Los Angeles shows a different pattern, where Asian and Pacific Islander individuals appear overrepresented in stops, and people classified as “other” are underrepresented. In Nashville, the proportion of stopped Black individuals is noticeably higher than their share of the population, suggesting a potential racial bias in policing.


Show code
#| fig-alt: A set of two bar charts comparing traffic stops in Austin by race, split into female and male subjects. Each chart shows counts for five racial groups: Asian or Pacific Islander, Black, Hispanic, Other, and White. White individuals have the highest number of stops in both groups, followed by Hispanic and Black individuals, with Asian/Pacific Islander and Other making up much smaller proportions.

# Plot number of stops in Austin by race, separated by sex
gender_austin |> 
  filter(!is.na(subject_race),subject_race != "unknown") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = subject_race, y = n, fill = subject_race)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ sex) +
  theme_bw() +
  # Remove x-axis labels
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.title.x = element_blank()

  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Paired") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Stopped Individuals in Austin by Race",
    y = "Number of stops",
    fill = "Race of Subject"
  )





Distribution of traffic stops in Austin by race and sex.




For the next part of the analysis, I looked at how the racial breakdown of stops changes when we split the data by gender. I focused on Austin for this comparison. Overall, the racial patterns look similar across men and women, but the total number of stops is consistently higher for men.


Show code
#| fig-alt: A faceted bar chart showing the average age of stopped individuals in Austin. The left panel shows females and the right panel shows males. For each sex, bars represent racial groups: Asian/Pacific Islander, Black, Hispanic, Other, and White. Ages mostly fall between 34 and 40, with male subjects generally slightly older across all groups, and white males having the highest average age.

# Plot average age by race, separated by sex
gender_age_austin |> 
  filter(!is.na(subject_race),subject_race != "unknown") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = subject_race, y = age, fill = subject_race)) +

    axis.text.x = element_blank(),

    title = "Average Age of Stopped Individual in Austin",

    fill = "Race of Subject"
  )+
  # Limit y-axis to 30–40
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(30, 40))





Average age of stopped individuals in Austin, separated by race and sex.




I also examined the average age of stopped individuals in Austin by both race and gender. Among women, Black individuals had the highest average age, followed by white individuals. For men, this pattern flips, with white individuals having the highest average age instead. Overall, the average age is slightly lower for women, ranging from 33.6 (unknown) to 36.5 (Black), compared to men, whose averages range from 35.7 (Asian/Pacific Islander) to 39.8 (white).


Conclusion
Terminating SQL connection:


Show code
dbDisconnect(con_traffic)


Overall, this project combined SQL wrangling, external population data, and data visualization to explore how demographic factors show up in traffic stops. The goal was to move from simple counts to a more contextual understanding by comparing stop patterns to who actually lives in each city. Focusing on Austin also showed how gender and age add another layer to these differences.

CensusDots. “Austin, TX Demographics.” https://www.censusdots.com/race/austin-tx-demographics.
CensusDots. “Los Angeles County, CA Demographics.” https://www.censusdots.com/race/los-angeles-county-ca-demographics.
CensusDots. “Nashville–Davidson Metropolitan Government Balance, TN Demographics.” https://www.censusdots.com/race/nashville-davidson-metropolitan-government-balance-tn-demographics.

title: Permutation Test
text:
The dataset, Students Data Analysis, contains information on students’ graduation acceptances (did not get into the graduate school, got into a local graduate school, got into a international graduate school) and their assigned class (class), a categorical variable with two groups. Students were initially divided into two classes, but instructors suspected that students in one class might be performing significantly differently from those in the other.
To test this hypothesis, I will use a permutation test to compare acceptance rates between the two classes. The procedure involved repeatedly shuffling the class labels while keeping the graduation scores fixed, then calculating the mean difference in graduation rates for each permutation. This generated a null distribution representing the differences we would expect if class assignment had no real effect on performance.
IMPORTANT NOTE: The dataset used in this analysis is half-synthetic, meaning that although it was originally based on student records, the variables have been anonymized, censored, and partially generated to protect privacy. As a result, the class categories do not represent real student groups, and the patterns observed in the data may not reflect any real-world population. The analysis here should therefore be interpreted purely as a practice exercise for understanding and applying permutation tests.

Hypotheses
Null hypothesis (H₀): There is no difference in graduate school acceptance rates between the two classes. Any observed difference is due to random chance.
Alternative hypothesis (Hₐ): There is a difference in graduate school acceptance rates between the two classes.
Loading the dataset and packages:


Show code
library(RTextTools) 
library(tidyverse)
library(stringr)
library(readr)
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)
library(gt)
students <- read.csv("Students Data.csv")




Step 1: Explore and Summarize the Dataset
Because the dataset includes two types of graduate school acceptances (international and local) I combined them into a single category and calculated the average graduation acceptance rate.


Show code
# Create binary grad variable and keep class and grad columns
students_clean <- students |> 
  mutate(grad = as.integer(y>0)) |> 
  select(class, grad) 

# Calculate acceptance proportion by class and display table
students_clean |> 
  group_by(class) |> 
  summarize(ave_grad = mean(grad)) |> 
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(
    title = "Average Grad School Acceptances by Class"
  ) 








Average Grad School Acceptances by Class


class
ave_grad




A
0.5131579


B
0.3793103









Show code
# Compute difference in acceptance proportions between the two classes
students_clean |> 
  group_by(class) |> 
  # proportion accepted per class
  summarize(ave_grad = mean(grad)) |> 
  # difference: Class B - Class A
  summarize(ave_diff =diff(ave_grad)) |> 
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Differences in Grad School Acceptances Between Classes"
  )








Differences in Grad School Acceptances Between Classes


ave_diff




-0.1338475







From the analysis, we can see that Class A had a higher graduate school acceptance rate than Class B.
Before conducting the permutation test, we can visualize the proportion of students accepted to graduate school in each class. This helps contextualize the observed difference in acceptance rates.


Show code
# Show proportion (mean) of grad acceptance by class
students_clean |> 
  group_by(class) |> 
  summarize(prop_accept = mean(grad)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = class, y = prop_accept, fill = class)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(
    title = "Proportion of Students Accepted to Graduate School by Class",
    x = "Class",
    y = "Proportion Accepted"
  ) +
  theme_light()





Proportion of students accepted to graduate school in each class.






Step 2: Permutation Test Function
This function tests whether the difference in the proportion of students accepted to graduate school between the two classes could have occurred by chance alone. Because grad is coded as 0 or 1, the average within each class represents the proportion accepted. The test works by shuffling the grad values across students, recalculating the difference in acceptance proportions for each permutation, and comparing those values to the observed difference. This produces both the observed statistic (ave_diff) and a distribution of permuted statistics (perm_diff). I set a random seed to ensure reproducibility and used map() to repeat the permutation process 1,000 times, storing all results in a data frame called perm_stats.


Show code
#a function that computes the observed and permuted differences
grad_diff <- function(rep, students_clean) {
  students_clean |> 
    # shuffle grad values
    mutate(grad_perm = sample(grad, replace = FALSE)) |> 
    group_by(class) |> 
    summarize(
       # observed proportion
      obs_ave = mean(grad),
      # permuted proportion
      perm_ave = mean(grad_perm)) |> 
    summarize(
      # observed difference
      ave_diff =diff(obs_ave), 
      # permuted difference
      perm_diff = diff(perm_ave), 
      # iterate label
      rep = rep)
}

# Run the permutation test 1000 times
set.seed(47)
number <- 1000
perm_stats<- map(c(1:number), grad_diff, students_clean) |> 
  list_rbind()




Step 3: Visualize the Null Distribution
The histogram below displays this null distribution of permuted mean differences (perm_diff), with the red line showing the observed mean difference from the original data (ave_diff).


Show code
perm_stats |> 
  # histogram of permuted differences
  ggplot(aes(x = perm_diff))+
  geom_histogram(bins  = 40 ,fill = "skyblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
  # Add title and axis labels
  labs(
    title = "Permutation Distribution of Mean Differences",
    subtitle = "Red line = observed difference",
    x = "Permutation Mean Difference",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  # mark observed difference
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = ave_diff), color = "red", linewidth = 1.2)+
  theme_classic()+
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )





Permutation distribution of the difference in graduate school acceptance proportions between the two classes.




From the plot, we can see that the red line, which represents the observed difference, is slightly to one side of the null distribution. However, it does not seem far enough from the center to suggest a meaningful or statistically significant difference at first glance.


Step 4: Calculate the p-value
Finally, I calculated the p-value


Show code
# Compute the two-sided p-value:
perm_stats |> 
  summarize(p_val_ave = mean(abs(perm_diff) >= abs(ave_diff))) |>
  gt() |> 
  tab_header(
    title = "Left-tailed p-value"
  )








Left-tailed p-value


p_val_ave




0.285







Because this is a two-sided test, the p-value was computed as the proportion of permuted differences whose absolute value was greater than or equal to the absolute observed difference.


Step 5: Results
The permutation test produced a p-value greater than 0.05, meaning the observed difference in graduate school acceptance proportions between the two classes is not statistically significant. In other words, the difference we see could easily have arisen by random chance, so we fail to reject the null hypothesis (H₀). Based on this analysis, there isn’t enough evidence to conclude that class assignment meaningfully affects graduate school acceptance within this dataset.
Citation:

Zhou, Erqi. Students Data Analysis. Synthetic dataset created from anonymized student records.
Zhou, Erqi. Students Data Analysis. Kaggle, 2024. https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/erqizhou/students-data-analysis.
